PROJECT 1
Laser Surveillance Microphone
Hear through a window from 100m — no mic in the room, no RF, no trace

Cost: ~$15
Difficulty: Advanced
Build Time: 1-2 weekends
Why This Matters
During the Cold War, intelligence agencies developed laser listening devices that could extract audio
from vibrating surfaces at distance. The principle is simple: sound waves inside a room cause the
window glass to vibrate by nanometers. An IR laser bouncing off that window is phase-modulated by
the vibration. A sensitive photodetector reads that modulation, and an FM demodulator extracts the
audio. The technique was declassified decades ago, but the analog design challenges remain:
sub-millivolt signal detection, laser intensity stabilization, and FM demodulation of an extremely weak
carrier.
What this proves to a recruiter: You understand optical signal chains, laser driver
design, transimpedance amplification at the noise floor, and analog FM
demodulation. These skills directly apply to LIDAR, fiber optics, optical sensing, and
defense.
System Architecture
@1nska  •  Defense Tech Part 2: Laser + Covert Systems  •  Page 3
How It Works
• IR laser diode (808nm): A collimated infrared laser aimed at a window pane. The laser must be
intensity-stabilized using an APC (automatic power control) circuit — a monitor photodiode inside
the laser package feeds back to the driver, keeping output power constant. Any intensity drift
appears as noise in the received signal.
• Window vibration: Sound waves inside the room cause the glass to vibrate. A normal
conversation at 60dB SPL causes ~1-10nm of displacement on a window pane. This displacement
phase-modulates the reflected laser beam — the path length changes by twice the displacement
(there and back), creating a Doppler shift proportional to the velocity of the glass surface.
• Photodetector + TIA: A large-area silicon photodiode (BPW34 or similar) with a transimpedance
amplifier (1MΩ feedback) captures the reflected beam. The DC component represents the average
reflected power. The AC component (microvolts) carries the audio information. A coupling
capacitor separates them.
• Bandpass filter (300Hz-3kHz): A 4th-order Sallen-Key bandpass isolates the speech band. This
removes laser noise below 300Hz and high-frequency detector noise above 3kHz.
• FM demodulator: The phase modulation from the window vibration is equivalent to FM. A simple
PLL-based FM demodulator (LM567 or NE567) or a slope detector (tuned LC circuit on the slope
of the resonance curve) extracts the audio. Amplify and output to speaker or ADC.
Key Design Decisions
→ Why 808nm instead of visible laser? 808nm is invisible to the human eye — the target
doesn't know they're being illuminated. It also avoids eye safety concerns at low power levels and
matches common, cheap laser diodes.
→ Why APC on the laser driver? Without intensity stabilization, laser power fluctuations appear
as amplitude noise that masks the tiny phase modulation signal. The APC loop must have
bandwidth >10kHz to track fast intensity variations.
→ Why FM demodulation, not AM? The window vibration modulates the phase/frequency of the
reflected beam, not the amplitude. Amplitude changes come from beam wander and atmospheric
scintillation — these are noise sources, not signal. FM demodulation rejects AM noise inherently.

Build Steps
Laser transmitter: Mount 808nm laser diode in a collimating lens assembly. Build an APC driver:
LM317 as current source, monitor photodiode feedback through an op-amp comparator that
adjusts drive current to maintain constant output. Set power to 50-100mW — enough for reflection
from 100m but below eye-safety limits for diffuse reflection. Mount on a tripod with fine adjustment
screws.
Optical receiver: Large-area BPW34 photodiode with a 10mm focusing lens to collect the
reflected beam (which will be spread over a large area at 100m). TIA with 1MΩ feedback + 1pF
compensation cap. Add a narrowband optical filter (800-820nm) in front of the lens to reject
ambient light. Shield the entire receiver in a tube to reject stray light from the sides.
Signal conditioning: AC-couple the TIA output through 100nF. First stage: x100 amplification.
Second stage: Sallen-Key bandpass 300Hz-3kHz (4th order for sharp rolloff). Verify on
oscilloscope: with the laser on a nearby window and someone talking, you should see an AC
waveform correlated with the speech.
FM demodulation: Feed the filtered signal into an LM567 PLL configured as an FM demodulator.
Set the free-running frequency to match the carrier (center of your bandpass). The demodulated
output is a voltage proportional to the instantaneous frequency deviation — this IS the audio
signal. Low-pass at 3kHz and amplify for speaker output.
@1nska  •  Defense Tech Part 2: Laser + Covert Systems  •  Page 5
Test and calibrate: Start with a short range test (5m, indoors). Aim laser at a window. Play music
inside the room near the window. You should hear the music through your receiver. Increase range
gradually — 10m, 20m, 50m, 100m. At each range, adjust the receiver gain and verify SNR.
Document the maximum intelligible range and the SNR vs distance curve.
Interview Questions:
→ How does sound inside a room modulate a laser beam reflected off the window?
→ Why is automatic power control critical for the laser driver?
→ What limits the maximum range of this system?
→ How does FM demodulation reject amplitude noise from atmospheric effects?
→ What countermeasures exist against laser microphone surveillance?
→ How would you improve sensitivity — what's the theoretical noise floor?

PROJECT 2
Tap-Proof Laser Communication Link
Encrypted data over invisible IR beam — no RF emission, cannot be intercepted
Cost: ~$12

Difficulty:
Intermediate-Advanced
Build Time: 1-2 weekends
Why This Matters
Every radio transmission can be intercepted, direction-found, and jammed. Laser communication
eliminates all three problems: the beam is directional (impossible to intercept from the side), invisible
(808nm IR), and carries no RF signature. Military Special Operations, submarine-to-satellite links, and
inter-spacecraft communication all use optical links for exactly these reasons. This project builds a
complete encrypted optical link: modulated laser transmitter, avalanche photodiode receiver, clock
recovery, and AES encryption.
System Architecture
@1nska  •  Defense Tech Part 2: Laser + Covert Systems  •  Page 7
How It Works
• Transmitter — laser driver with OOK modulation: An 808nm laser diode driven by a MOSFET
switching circuit. On-Off Keying (OOK): laser on = 1, laser off = 0. The MCU (ESP32) encrypts the
data with AES-128, adds start/stop framing and Manchester encoding (for clock recovery), then
drives the MOSFET at up to 1 Mbps.
• Receiver — avalanche photodiode (APD): An APD (or high-speed PIN diode like SFH213)
provides internal gain through avalanche multiplication. This gives 10-50x better sensitivity than a
standard photodiode. Biased at just below breakdown voltage (typically 100-150V from a boost
converter). The received photocurrent feeds a transimpedance amplifier.
• Clock recovery: Manchester encoding ensures a transition in every bit period, allowing the
receiver's PLL to synchronize its clock to the transmitter's bit rate. Without clock recovery, timing
drift over long messages causes bit errors. A simple DPLL (digital PLL) implemented on the
ESP32 handles this.
• AES decryption: The receiver ESP32 strips framing, decodes Manchester, and decrypts
AES-128 using a pre-shared key stored in flash. Output: original plaintext on serial terminal or
OLED display.

Build Steps
Transmitter: ESP32 GPIO drives 2N7000 MOSFET gate through 100Ω resistor. MOSFET drain to
laser diode cathode through current-limiting resistor (set for rated current). Laser anode to VCC.
Test: toggle GPIO at 1kHz — verify laser blinks with oscilloscope and photodiode. Then implement
Manchester encoding: each '1' bit = high-then-low transition, each '0' = low-then-high. Add
AES-128 encryption using ESP32's hardware AES engine.
Receiver optics: Mount SFH213 photodiode behind a 25mm focusing lens. Add an 800-820nm
optical bandpass filter to reject ambient light. The lens focuses the incoming beam onto the small
active area of the diode, increasing the collected photon count. Shield the assembly in a tube
painted matte black inside.
Receiver electronics: TIA with 100kΩ feedback (lower than laser mic because we need
bandwidth for 1Mbps). Follow with a limiting amplifier or comparator (LM393) that converts the
analog signal to clean digital pulses. Feed to ESP32 GPIO input configured for interrupt-on-edge.
Clock recovery + decoding: ESP32 measures the time between each edge transition.
Manchester encoding guarantees a transition every bit period. A software DPLL adjusts the
sampling point to the center of each bit. Decode Manchester back to binary. Strip framing bytes.
Decrypt AES-128. Output plaintext to serial or OLED.
Range test: Start at 10m indoors. Transmit a known message, verify error-free reception. Increase
to 50m, 100m, 200m. At each distance, measure BER (bit error rate) by transmitting 10,000 known
bits and counting errors. Document BER vs distance. In clear air, you should achieve <10^-6 BER
at 200m with proper alignment.
Interview Questions:
→ Why is OOK modulation simpler than PSK for optical links?
→ How does Manchester encoding enable clock recovery at the receiver?
→ What limits the maximum data rate of this system?
→ Why can't this link be intercepted from the side?
→ How does atmospheric turbulence affect the link and how would you mitigate it?
→ Compare this to RF communication — advantages and disadvantages of each.

PROJECT 3
Laser Rangefinder
Time-of-flight distance measurement with 5ns pulse and 100ps timing resolution

Cost: ~$25
Difficulty: Advanced
Build Time: 1-2 weekends
Why This Matters
Every military targeting system, every autonomous vehicle LIDAR, every surveying instrument uses
laser time-of-flight ranging. The principle is simple: fire a short laser pulse, start a timer, stop it when
the reflection arrives, calculate distance from the round-trip time. The implementation is one of the
hardest analog design challenges in EE: generating nanosecond pulses, building a time-to-digital
converter with picosecond resolution, and designing a receiver sensitive enough to detect photons
reflected from hundreds of meters away.
Why this is the ultimate portfolio project: A working laser rangefinder
demonstrates high-speed analog design, precision timing circuits, optical
engineering, and signal processing — all in one device. It's the project that makes
interviewers stop asking standard questions and start having a technical
conversation.
System Architecture
@1nska  •  Defense Tech Part 2: Laser + Covert Systems  •  Page 10
How It Works
• Pulse generator (5ns): A MOSFET avalanche pulser circuit. A high-voltage supply (100-200V)
charges a small capacitor through a resistor. When the MOSFET is triggered, the cap discharges
through the laser diode in nanoseconds. The avalanche breakdown of the MOSFET provides the
fast switching edge. Pulse width is determined by the capacitance and parasitic inductance —
keep leads short.
• Laser diode (905nm): A pulsed laser diode rated for high peak power (10-75W) but low average
power (duty cycle <0.1%). 905nm is standard for rangefinders because it's eye-safe at the power
levels used and atmospheric absorption is low. A collimating lens focuses the beam to <1 mrad
divergence.
• Receiver (APD): An avalanche photodiode with a narrowband 905nm filter and focusing optics.
The APD provides internal gain (x50-200) at a reverse bias of 100-200V. A transimpedance
amplifier converts the photocurrent pulse to a voltage pulse. A comparator with adjustable
threshold generates the STOP signal for the TDC.
• Time-to-Digital Converter (TDC): The heart of the system. The laser trigger pulse is the START
signal. The APD comparator output is the STOP signal. The TDC measures the time between
them. A TDC7200 IC provides 55ps resolution. Alternatively, build a Vernier delay line TDC from
discrete logic — two ring oscillators at slightly different frequencies that achieve interpolated timing
down to ~100ps.
• Distance calculation: Distance = (time × c) / 2, where c = 3×10I m/s. At 100ps resolution:
distance resolution = (100ps × 3×10I) / 2 = 1.5 cm. Average multiple measurements to reduce
noise and improve resolution further.

Build Steps
Avalanche pulser: Charge a 100pF capacitor to 200V through a 10MΩ resistor (slow charge,
~1ms). IRF510 MOSFET gate driven by a fast logic signal (3.3V from MCU through gate driver).
When the MOSFET switches, the cap dumps into the laser diode through minimal inductance
(short, wide traces). The pulse width is determined by the LC ringing — aim for 5-10ns. Measure
with a fast oscilloscope (>500MHz bandwidth).
Laser optics: Mount the pulsed laser diode in a collimating lens tube. Adjust focus for minimum
beam divergence at 50m (use a wall as target). The RX optics: a 25mm lens focuses reflected
photons onto the APD active area. Mount TX and RX optics side by side with ~3cm separation
(bistatic configuration) or coaxially with a beam splitter (monostatic).
Receiver chain: APD biased at its rated voltage (check datasheet — typically 100-200V from a
boost converter). TIA with 10kΩ feedback (need bandwidth for 5ns pulse). Follow with a
high-speed comparator (LT1016 or ADCMP600) with adjustable threshold. The comparator output
is the STOP signal — a clean digital edge triggered by the received photon pulse.
TDC measurement: Connect the laser trigger to TDC7200 START input. Connect the comparator
output to STOP input. The TDC7200 communicates via SPI — read the time-interval register.
Convert to distance: d = (time_ns × 0.15) meters. Average 10 measurements for improved
precision. Display on OLED.
@1nska  •  Defense Tech Part 2: Laser + Covert Systems  •  Page 12
Calibration and test: Start with a known distance (measure with tape). Compare rangefinder
reading to actual distance. Adjust the fixed time offset (cable delays, processing delays). Then test
at multiple distances: 5m, 10m, 20m, 50m, 100m. Plot measured vs actual distance. The slope
should be 1.000 ± 0.001. Document the maximum range (where SNR drops below threshold) and
the precision (standard deviation of repeated measurements at fixed distance).
Interview Questions:
→ Explain the avalanche pulser circuit — how do you generate a 5ns pulse?
→ What determines the minimum and maximum measurable distance?
→ How does the TDC achieve picosecond resolution from a MHz clock?
→ What limits the range of your system — is it peak power, receiver sensitivity, or
optics?
→ How would you implement multi-target detection (seeing through glass, for
example)?
→ What eye safety considerations apply to this design?

PROJECT 4
Encrypted Burst Transmitter

50ms frequency-hopping burst — too fast to DF, too short to jam, encrypted if
intercepted

Cost: ~$10
Difficulty: Intermediate
Build Time: 1-2 weekends
Why This Matters
In electronic warfare, the three threats to radio communication are: interception (listening), direction
finding (locating the transmitter), and jamming (disrupting the signal). A burst transmitter defeats all
three. The message is compressed and encrypted, then transmitted in a single 50ms burst on a
pseudo-random frequency. 50ms is too short for most direction-finding systems to get a bearing.
Frequency hopping means a jammer doesn't know which frequency to block. AES encryption means
even if the burst is recorded, it can't be read. This is the fundamental operating principle of military
SINCGARS and HAVE QUICK radios.
System Architecture
@1nska  •  Defense Tech Part 2: Laser + Covert Systems  •  Page 14
How It Works
• Message input: User types a text message on the ESP32 serial terminal (up to 256 characters).
The MCU compresses the text using run-length encoding (saves ~30% on typical messages) and
encrypts with AES-256 using a pre-shared key.
• FHSS sequence generation: A pseudo-random number generator (seeded with a shared
secret) generates a sequence of frequencies across the ISM band (902-928 MHz for US, or 433
MHz band). The TX and RX use the same seed, so they hop to the same frequencies at the same
time.
• Si4432 RF module: A frequency-agile transceiver that can retune in <100µs. The MCU sends
the encrypted, compressed packet in a single 50ms burst. During the burst, the frequency hops
every 5ms across 10 channels. Total airtime per channel: 5ms — below the threshold of most
spectrum analyzers and DF systems.
• Receiver: An identical Si4432 + ESP32 module, time-synchronized with the transmitter (either
GPS-disciplined clocks or a pre-agreed hop schedule). The receiver hops through the same
frequency sequence, collecting 5ms fragments and reassembling the full packet. Decrypt and
display.

Build Steps
Basic RF link: Wire two Si4432 modules to two ESP32s via SPI. Verify basic communication:
send a test message from TX, receive on RX. Measure range with simple continuous transmission
— should be 500m+ with wire antenna line-of-sight.
Compression + encryption: Implement RLE compression on the TX ESP32. Then implement
AES-256 encryption using the ESP32's hardware AES engine. Pre-share a 256-bit key (flash it to
both devices during programming). Verify: transmit an encrypted message, decrypt on the
receiver, compare to original.
Frequency hopping: Implement the PRNG-based hop sequence. Both TX and RX use the same
seed, so they generate the same frequency list. Program the Si4432 to retune every 5ms across
10 frequencies within the ISM band. The Si4432's frequency resolution is 156Hz, so you can hop
precisely. Test: use an RTL-SDR as a spectrum analyzer to observe the signal jumping across
frequencies.
Burst assembly: Instead of continuous transmission, the MCU buffers the entire encrypted,
compressed message. On button press: the MCU transmits the entire packet in one 50ms burst,
hopping 10 times during the burst. Total airtime: 50ms. Then radio silence. The receiver collects all
10 fragments and reassembles.
Time synchronization: For the receiver to hop in sync with the transmitter, both need a shared
time reference. Simplest method: both devices start their hop sequence from a pre-agreed time
offset after power-on (e.g., aligned to the nearest second using an RTC module). More advanced:
GPS-disciplined oscillator for sub-microsecond sync.
Interview Questions:
→ How does frequency hopping prevent jamming?
→ Why is 50ms too short for direction finding — what DF methods exist and what are
their time requirements?
→ How do you synchronize the transmitter and receiver hop sequences?
→ What's the tradeoff between burst length and message capacity?
→ How does your PRNG sequence ensure spectral spreading?
→ Compare FHSS to DSSS (direct-sequence spread spectrum) — advantages of
each.

PROJECT 5
Passive Night Vision Scope
Image amplification from ambient starlight — zero emission, fully covert

Cost: ~$30
Difficulty: Advanced
Build Time: 1-2 weekends
Why This Matters
Most commercial 'night vision' devices cheat — they blast IR LEDs and use a camera. This is visible to
anyone else with night vision and broadcasts your position. Real military night vision (Gen III image
intensifiers) amplifies ambient photons — starlight, moonlight, airglow — without emitting anything.
This project builds a digital equivalent: a high-sensitivity CMOS sensor with a fast lens, gain-adjustable
analog front end, and OLED microdisplay eyepiece. No IR illuminator. No emission. Fully passive.
System Architecture
How It Works
• Fast lens (f/1.0): The lens determines how many photons reach the sensor. An f/1.0 lens collects
4x more light than an f/2.0 lens. CCTV lenses with 25mm focal length and f/1.0-f/1.2 aperture are
available for $5-10. This is the single most important component — without a fast lens, no amount
of electronic gain will produce a usable image.
• CMOS sensor (OV7251): A global-shutter monochrome sensor with high NIR sensitivity.
Monochrome sensors are 3-4x more sensitive than color sensors (no Bayer filter absorbing 2/3 of
the photons). The OV7251 has 3µm pixels with good quantum efficiency at 850-950nm — where
@1nska  •  Defense Tech Part 2: Laser + Covert Systems  •  Page 17
night sky airglow provides ambient illumination.
• Gain control (AGC): The sensor's analog gain is adjustable from 1x to 64x. An AGC loop adjusts
the gain based on average image brightness — in darker conditions, gain increases automatically.
Additional digital gain (2-8x) on the processor trades noise for visibility in extreme darkness.
• Image processor (STM32H7 or RPi Zero): Reads the sensor via MIPI CSI or parallel interface.
Applies histogram equalization to maximize contrast. Optionally applies noise reduction (temporal
averaging of 2-4 frames). Outputs to OLED microdisplay.
• OLED microdisplay: A 0.39" or 0.5" OLED microdisplay viewed through an eyepiece lens.
Green phosphor color (matches human scotopic sensitivity) for traditional NV appearance. Refresh
rate: 30fps minimum to avoid flicker.

Build Steps
Optical assembly: Mount the f/1.0 lens on the OV7251 camera module using a CS-mount
adapter. Verify focus at infinity (point at a distant streetlight at night). The image should be sharp
and bright through the viewfinder. If using an RPi camera module instead of bare OV7251, remove
the IR-cut filter — this dramatically increases NIR sensitivity.
Sensor configuration: Configure the OV7251 (or RPi camera) for maximum sensitivity: longest
exposure time that maintains 30fps (33ms), maximum analog gain (64x), monochrome mode (no
demosaicing). Capture test images at night — compare exposure settings systematically to find the
optimal gain/exposure tradeoff for your lighting conditions.
Image processing pipeline: On the RPi Zero: capture frames at 30fps. Apply CLAHE (Contrast
Limited Adaptive Histogram Equalization) to maximize local contrast. Optionally average 2-4
consecutive frames to reduce temporal noise (at the cost of motion blur). Convert to green-tinted
grayscale for traditional NV appearance.
@1nska  •  Defense Tech Part 2: Laser + Covert Systems  •  Page 18
Display output: Route the processed image to the OLED microdisplay via SPI. The display sits at
the focal point of the eyepiece lens — the eye sees a virtual image at infinity. Adjust the eyepiece
position until the image is sharp and comfortable to view. The total magnification is determined by
the ratio of the objective focal length to the eyepiece focal length.
Field test: Test in progressively darker conditions: dusk → street-lit area → moonlit rural area →
starlight only. Document the minimum illumination level at which objects are recognizable.
Compare to your phone camera at the same location. A well-built passive NV scope should
outperform a phone camera by 10-20x in low light due to the fast lens, monochrome sensor, and
histogram equalization.

PROJECT 6
Radar Cross-Section Measurement System
Test stealth shapes and radar-absorbing materials at your desk

Cost: ~$12
Difficulty: Intermediate
Build Time: 1-2 weekends
Why This Matters
Radar cross-section (RCS) is the measure of how visible an object is to radar. A large RCS means
easy to detect; a small RCS means stealthy. Every stealth aircraft, ship, and vehicle is designed to
minimize RCS through shape (angling surfaces away from the radar) and materials (absorbing radar
energy instead of reflecting it). This project builds a bistatic RCS measurement system using two
HB100 modules — one as transmitter, one as receiver — that lets you measure RCS reduction of
different shapes and coatings at 10.5 GHz. You're doing what Lockheed does in anechoic chambers,
on your desk.
System Architecture
@1nska  •  Defense Tech Part 2: Laser + Covert Systems  •  Page 20
How It Works
• TX module (HB100): Transmits continuous wave at 10.525 GHz. Mount facing the target area.
The HB100 outputs approximately 15dBm (30mW) — enough for measurements at 1-3m range in
a desktop setup. Add a small horn antenna (cut from a tin can) to focus the beam and reduce
clutter from reflections off the desk/walls.
• RX module (second HB100): A second HB100 used as a receiver. The HB100's mixer output
gives a signal proportional to the received 10.5GHz power. Mount at 90° or 180° to the TX (bistatic
or forward-scatter configuration). The mixer IF output is amplified and measured.
• Reference measurement: First, measure the received power with a known reference target — a
metal sphere of known diameter. The RCS of a sphere is σ = π × r² (geometric cross-section). This
calibrates the system: you know the relationship between received power and RCS in dBsm.
• Test targets: Now replace the reference sphere with your test objects: a flat plate at various
angles, a faceted shape (like a stealth aircraft cross-section), a foam shape coated with
carbon-loaded paint (RAM — radar absorbing material). Measure received power for each.
Calculate RCS relative to the reference. Express the reduction in dB.

Build Steps
TX setup: Mount HB100 TX module on a stable platform. Build a simple horn antenna from a tin
can (75mm diameter, 100mm length) — solder the HB100's patch antenna centered at the mouth
of the can. This provides ~10dB of directional gain, focusing the beam on the target area and
reducing wall reflections.
RX setup: Mount the second HB100 at the receive position (1-2m away, same height, facing the
target area). Connect the IF output to a TL072 non-inverting amplifier with gain of x100. Follow with
a low-pass filter at 100Hz (to average the received power). Feed to ADS1115 ADC read by an
Arduino.
Reference calibration: Place a 25mm steel ball bearing at the target position (centered between
TX and RX). Record the received power (ADC reading). This is your reference RCS. The
theoretical RCS of a 25mm sphere at 10.5GHz: σ = π × (0.0125)² = 4.9 × 10II m² = -33 dBsm. All
subsequent measurements are relative to this reference.
Test stealth shapes: Cut foam into different shapes: flat plate (high RCS), 45° angled plate
(deflects energy away), diamond shape (multiple facets), rounded shape (diffuses energy). Mount
each on a slow-rotation turntable (1 RPM). Record received power vs angle. Plot the RCS pattern
— you should see dramatic differences between a flat plate (bright return) and an angled shape
(greatly reduced return).
Test RAM coatings: Take a flat foam plate (high RCS baseline). Coat one side with
carbon-loaded paint (mix graphite powder into acrylic paint). Measure RCS of uncoated side, then
coated side. The carbon paint should absorb some radar energy, reducing the RCS by 3-10dB
depending on coating thickness and carbon loading. Experiment with different carbon
concentrations to find optimal absorption.
Interview Questions:
→ What is radar cross-section and what determines it?
→ Why use a sphere as a calibration reference?
→ How does object shape affect RCS — explain the principle behind stealth
geometry?
→ What physical mechanism causes carbon-loaded paint to absorb radar energy?
→ What's the difference between bistatic and monostatic RCS measurement?
→ How would you build a proper anechoic chamber to reduce measurement clutter?
